extracted.intended_audience: faculty, chapter members, and administrators at the University (AAUP-UC audience); higher-education faculty and union representatives
extracted.subtask_description: Core principles and standards describing academic freedom and shared governance for faculty and institutions, including related safeguards (tenure, compensation, responsibilities, due process) and the chapter's role in defending rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic Freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions of higher education are conducted for the common good and not to further the interest of either the individual teacher or the institution as a whole. The common good depends upon the free search for truth and its free exposition. The academic freedom of faculty members includes the freedom to express their views (1) on academic matters in the classroom and in the conduct of research, (2) on matters having to do with their institution and its policies, and (3) on issues of public interest generally, and to do so even if their views are in conflict with one or another received wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty must be free to teach, engage in research, and participate in institutional governance without fear of punishment or repercussions because their legitimate academic activities are politically controversial or unpopular. See AAUP 1940 Statement of Principles on Academic Freedom and Tenure and 1994 statement On the Relationship of Faculty Governance to Academic Freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of tenure was created to protect academic freedom. Tenure is a means to certain ends; specifically: (1) freedom of teaching and research and of extramural activities, and (2) a sufficient degree of economic security to make the profession attractive to men and women of ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tenure provides job security that supports freedom in teaching/research; in modern contexts, job-security protections should extend to non-tenure-track faculty where necessary to preserve academic freedom. See AAUP statements on Contingent Appointments and the Academic Profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate Compensation & Full-Time Employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate compensation is a requisite for the health of the faculty as a whole. Academic freedom and freedom from fear of retaliation are protected not only by tenure, but also by financial security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy reliance on part-time or poorly compensated adjunct faculty undermines academic freedom because faculty may avoid controversial teaching or research to protect income; economic security supports excellence and the ability to pursue controversial academic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic freedom does not mean faculty have no responsibility to students, peers, or their employer. Students should never have legitimate reason to believe that political beliefs—theirs or their professors’—will influence their grades. Faculty should respect the political viewpoints of their students and their peers, and ensure students are not required to adopt particular viewpoints while being responsible for knowing facts and issues and articulating them clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty must balance freedom with professional obligations: allow rigorous discussion but avoid imposing views; follow departmental curriculum authority and academic standards. See AAUP Freedom in the Classroom (2007) and AAUP-UC contract Article 3: Academic Safeguards and Responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Academic Freedom: Curriculum Authority and Evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic freedom does not mean faculty are completely free to teach whatever they like in any manner they like. The existence and authority of department curriculum committees are consistent with academic freedom. Faculty who are experts in the field have the primary authority, as a group, to set academic standards and curricular plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrations may set performance standards in cooperation with faculty; periodic evaluations should serve faculty development. The AAUP opposes using post-tenure review as a substitute for development-focused evaluations or as a mechanism to reevaluate tenured status. See AAUP-UC contract Article 27.2 and AAUP guidance on Post-Tenure Review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic freedom requires that faculty accused of being unable or unwilling to perform their duties (or of other serious charges) be given due process to prevent unfair, baseless, or politically motivated accusations from resulting in discipline or dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tenured faculty can be disciplined/fired for failure to perform, but procedures must ensure fair process; see AAUP-UC contract Article 9 for embodied due-process protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared Governance
rubrics_metrics.description: The public good is best served by viewing the academic institution as a cooperative effort among all components of the institutions, including the trustees, the administration, the students, and the faculty. The variety and complexity of institutional tasks produce inescapable interdependence among governing board, administration, faculty, students, and others, calling for adequate communication and full opportunity for appropriate joint planning and effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared governance is enacted at every level (academic unit, college, university) through mechanisms such as the University Faculty Senate. Article 27 of the AAUP-UC contract summarizes this vision and specifies faculty participation rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty Authority over Admissions, Academic Standards, and Curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty have 'the power to make their own regulations' regarding issues of student admissions, academic standards and other fundamental issues of curriculum. Faculty also have the right to 'share significantly in the responsibilities for' program, department, and college development and review, or reorganization; and the framing and execution of long-range plans, including but not limited to budget planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rights are to be exercised by faculty bodies (departments, senates); administration and trustees must recognize and consult with faculty on such matters as part of shared governance (see AAUP-UC contract Article 27).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Difference between Policy and Principle; Chapter's Role in Defending Governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Core principles (academic freedom and shared governance) are unchanging; policies (e.g., merit pay, compensation models) are negotiable and may change. The Chapter is not involved in the exercise of shared governance rights (e.g., RPT decisions, curriculum decisions); faculty execute those rights. The Chapter becomes involved only when faculty report violations and then assists faculty in asserting and exercising those rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish principle (guiding, enduring) from policy (context-dependent bargaining positions). The Chapter's role is defensive and supportive—helping faculty assert rights when violations are reported—not to replace faculty execution of governance functions.
